From the New York Commercial Advertiser' July 12, 1838. THE CAM ADAS. The Quebec Gazette of Friday contains a proclamation issued by l.ord Durham on the 3rd, revoking the proclamation issued by Lord Gosford, in which rewards were offered fur the apprehension of Messrs. Papineau, Brown and others, their apprehension, being no longer requisite for the ends of justice.

We arc enabled to inform our readers that there is not a word of truth in this last rumor; and what is more, that all the recent stories about invasion from Michigan, risings in the London District, <fco. are entirely destitute of foundation. We have seen a gentleman this morning, just from Upper Gauada, who informs us that there has been no fighting no invasion, and no disturbance, since the Short Hills affiiir, except on paper. The secret of the matter is simply this: þÿ Sir John Golhorne had ordered the militia to be disbanded on the 1st of July; but this did not suit the views of certain parties, and the whole story was got up to prevent the disbanding. þÿ Some eight hundred or nine hundred troops were marched of!, post hasts, to the Western dis-

tricts, and when they got there lo, there was not the least occasion for their presence, and all they had to do was to march hack again. The arrival of Lord Durham in Upper Ganada is anxiously looked for by the real friends of the province. We confidently an ticipate a quieting of all trouble from the wise and honest measures of the Governor General. The Buffalo Commercial of Mondav brings a rumor that Sir George Arthur has resigned, inconsequence of the amnesty proclaimed by Lord Durham. We need hardly say that it requires a great deal of confirmation.

STEAM SHIP GREAT WESTERN, Of the two United States Naval Officers who embarked in the Great. Western on her voyage out and home, we yesterday published from one of them, Lieut. Lynch a letter to Captain Hoskf.n, of a character highly complimentary to him and his vessel We have now the pleasure to add one from his companion, Lieut Carpender, as creditable to the writer as it also is flattering to the Steam Ship and her Commander. New York, June 20th, 1838. Dear Sir : þÿ 1 see bv the papers, this evening, on my return from Washington, that mv friend Mr Lynch, has left behind him a testimonial to Captain Hosken and the Great Western which, as a fellow-passenger, I have the greatest pleasure in responding to. It was with the utmost confidence in tire success of the undertaking that 1 was originally, an applicant for permission to cross the Atlantic, in order to make the first passage in the Great Western. Circumstances prevented me from gratifying my wish, but subsequently, through the liberality of the Directors of the Great Western Steam Uhip Company, and the accommodation afforded me bv mv government, 1 have been enabled to witness the performance of the Great Western at sea. J take this opportunity to return my thanks for the pleasure and satisfaction I have enjoyed. After an absence of only forty three days, 1 have visited England, spent ten davs therei returned with despatches to my government, delivered them and am now, unfntiguud by any portion of my journey, at my residence

in this city. The whole distance travelled, must he about seven thousand miles. This, I think, wilt be enough to satisfy the public and the world, if they have any longer any doubts on the subject, that really a new era has arrived, and that a life which was once short is now rendered long by the increased enjoyment which may he compressed within its limits. With the ship, the machine ry, and these results before all eyes, it would be superfluous in me to enlarge upon a topic already intelligible to the mind of everv one. I may only express my firm belief that steam navigation, both with the government and individuals, is destined to advance, and that through its means a union of the world, and an international respect, is likely to tnlse place, which will be productive of increased happiness to the whole human family. With every acknowledgment for vour kind and friendly attention, and that id Captain Hosken and the directors of the Company, 1 am, dear sir, very truly and sincerely Yours, E. W. CARPENDER. Richard Iimx, Esq. Consignee of the Steam Ship Great Western New York.

St. Croix, CHKISTIA NSTKI), ( MOM DA Y) August 27, 1838. London dates to the 17th July are received pr: second July Packet. Parliament were expected adjourn early August. to in The Irish municipal corporation bill had passed the House of Commons ; þÿ Sir It. Peel's amendment to substitute a ten pound qualification in lieu of five pounds was negatived and lost by a majority of 35; þÿ but in the House of Lords the ten pound qualification has been carried by a large majority. A brilliant review of the Household Cavalry, Infantry and Royal Artillery, by Her Majesty, took place in llvde Park on the 8th July, the Duke of Wellington, Marshal Soult, and all the distinguished Strangers in London were present þÿ the troops went thro' many evolutions and firings with great rapidity and precision, so much so as to excite the admiration of the distinguished military visitors who were present. The Lord Mayor made a grand dinner for the Foreign Ambassadors, the Duke of Wellington and Marshal Soult, on their health's being drunk reciprocally complimented each other in the highest terms. A succession of brilliant parties given by the Queen, Foreign Ambassadors, and leading Nobility, had followed the coronation. The London papers state that Marshal Soult on accepting the station of Ambassador extraordinary to the Queen of England, exacted from Louis Phillippe, as the condition of acceptance, that he should demand the remains of Napoleon from the British Government, to be conveyed to France from St. Helena ; þÿ to which they have acceeded ; þÿ the Duke of

Wellington having supported the demand of Marshal Soult. A French Frigate was to be dispatched to St. Helena for this purpose accompanied by a son of Louis Phillippe, and two soldiers from every French regiment were also to accompany the remains to France. Things looked threatning between Belgium and Holland þÿ a large Prussian and German Army were to occupy Luxemberg and Limbeig. In Spain Espartero continued to follow up his successes against Don Carlos, the latter appeared to be confined to the provinces of Biscay and Navarre, except some straggling maurauding parties pushed occasionally into the Southern provinces. The Great Western Steam Ship arrived at Bristol in 12 days and a half from New York ! The Prince De Joinvillehad arrived at Brest from the U. States. The dec ase of the Duke of Leeds in London is announced ; þÿ he is succeeded by the Marquis of Carmaethen, who married the widow of Colonel Harvey, þÿ she is a sister of the Marchioness of Wellesley, and was originally Miss Caton of Baltimore, U. S. a grand daughter of Charles Carroll of Carrollton, the last surviver of the signers of the declaration of Independence.

The Brig Eliza at Western! brings New York papers of the 1th inst., things remained quiet in Canada ; the Earl of Durham had lelumed to Quebec from Upper Canada, where his visit had been of much service. þÿ Commodore John Uodgers, senior officer in the U. S. Navy died at Philadelphia Aug. 2nd and he was buried with military hon-

ors. Commodore Rarron is now the senior officer in the Navy. Commodore Elliott has returned from the Mediterranean in the U S. Frigate Constitution, after an absence of 4 years. The British Steamer The Royal William arrived at New York from Liverpool in 18 days and had sailed again at a þÿ party given to the Mayor and Corporation of New York by the Commander of the Royal William, we observe that Captain Graah of H . D M. Brig St Thomas, lying at New York, was particularly noticed among the strangers ot distinction at the dinner. The Wheat crops were abundant in all parts of the U. States The warm weather continued, but no malignant fevers had been prevalent in any of the cities. Money affairs looked much better þÿ Exchange on London 107J þÿ a Branch of the U. S. Bank had been established in New York, and a grand Bank with branches through the State, was organizing at N. York, capital FIFTY MIL LIONS OF DOLLARS.

I availed myself of my worthy friend Mrs. W.,s invitation, to accompany her and her daughter to the Countess of Durham's fu st drawing room. Notice was given in all the papers as to the mode of procedure, and I confess I was pleased at the opportunity thus offered of attending the court of a Vice Queen. Nine o'clock was the hour appointed' A guard of honor was drawn up near the entrance of the chateau, as also a number of police. The eariiageshad all to fall in regular order An aid-de-camp in the splendid' indeed I may say gorgeous, attire of the royal guards, received us at the door, and we passed forward to where another aid-de-camp was in attendance, to whom I handed Mis. W 's card. We were then passed into the large ball room, which soon became filled with ladies and gentlemen. Among the latter were a great number of military and naval officers, many of them covered with stais and different orders. 'The ladies and gentlemen did not separate, as we do in New York nor yet stand still, but mingled together, exchanging kindly greetings and cheerful conversation. There were no chairs in the room. On entering the presence chamber we saw a tall and elegant lady standing out from a group which formed a kind of half circle, her station being about two yards in advance. þÿ the Jadv von handed to the room 'The ser- Near her stood the aid-de camp, splendidly dressed, to whom I handed Mrs. W.'s card, as directed, while she made her bow. 1 also

made mine, and she her second, and then taking my arm, we passed on. The Earl was standing alone, almost two yards from the Countess, and to him I bowed, which was returned, and on we went. 'The operation of passing through the room did not take up more than three minutes, or perhaps two. The whole presentation was over in little more than an hour. We passed to the hall and hack to the ball room, and after some conversation with various acquaintance, we passed down to the saloon, along each side and one end of which, full six feet from the wall, stood a broad elevated table, about four feet high, covered with fruits, ices,

lemonade and various liqueurs, wines, coffee, &c. «fec. There was no music, which would have been very agreeable to me, and the absence ot which was quite a disappointment ; but the drawing room was preparatory to a grand ball, and no music is allowed on sneh occasions. idastsk From the New York Evening Star, Sept: 4 Mr. John Van Buren was still residing in London, and receiving the most marked attention from the nobility and gentry. His name is reported in the Court Circular, as attending the þÿQueen s State Ball on the 19th of July ; and as one of the guests at a dinner given by the Turkish Ambassador on the following day. Mr. John Van Buren is now about twenty eight years of age. With some foibles and probably some frippery, he has passed through society as an agreeable and somewhat accomplished gentleman ; and adept at billiards and chess þÿ plays well and often at brag, whist, &c is a favourite among the ladies, and is a courteous, well bred young man. It is not generally known, however, that Mr. John Van Buren is a man of consider able political experience, dexterity and address, and his father has more confidence in his judgment than in all his other sons- The Coronation of the young Queen of England, and all the brilliancy and eclat connected with that imposing ceremony is seized upon by the President to address a letter of congratulation to the Queen, similar to the one Mr. Van Buren addressed to his Holiness, the Pope, which proved so profitable to him in the sequel This letter is sent by his eldest son þÿ the eldest son of the Chief Magistrate of a nation claiming rank with any nation on the face of the globe. The extraordinary and marked civilities and attention paid to him by the þÿQueen by the nobility by foreign þÿ the ambassadors, and bv the English Ministry, were not tributes to his

eminent talent, but to the fact that among the representatives of royalty brought to the British Court at the Coronation, was the eldest son and supposed þÿ heir apparent'" of the President of the United States. Mr. John Van Buren was not the representative of the free people of this country in any capacity, and yet his father, knowing this fact þÿ knowing that his own office was of limited tenure þÿ knowing that a few short fleeting tears would send him back to his little Farm on the Banks of the Hudson in obsecuritv, takes advantage of his office by placing his son in a position in England by which he shall be considered as heir apparent to the American Empire, receiving all those honors, and probably forming a matrimonial alliance with the daughter of a Peer of the Realm. All this may be very kind and parental on the part of Mr. Van Buren, but it is an improper use of his official influence and station þÿ injurious, as it can be shewn, to the interests of the country, and holding out false pretences under the cover of Executive power to promote private and selfish ends. As a citizen and a gentleman, all would rejoice it was the good fortune of Mr. John Van Buren to make himself acceptable to any lady of rank and fortune in England, but the son of the President þÿ that President having yet two years unexpired of his term, and making gigantic and most unprincipled efforts to secure a re-election, may form alliances in England among men of immense wealth, who may furnish the means which Mr. Van

Buren knows so well how to apply in certain sections to secure his re-election. Marry this þÿ heir apparent of the American þÿthrone to the dau 'liter of the Duke of Northumberland, of Devonshire, or of any rich commoner, and an interest will be forthwith created in England of no ordinary power to secure the re-election of Ins father. We learn from a gentleman lately arrived from Mexico, that the Government will continue to maintain a firm attitude in relation to the French blockade, neither receding nor advancing. We are told that the object of the Government in thus submitting to the blockade, is to direct, if possible, public attention to its resources, and establish a system of internal manufactures. Complele tranquillity appears to prevail at Mexico, but we learn from good authority that measures are even now in operation, which have for their object the elevation of Gomez Farias to the regency. This change of the administration will not, however, be attempted before the adjustment of the difficulties with France.

From the Alexandria Gazette. Jesse II Elliot, who by some freak of fortune, has risen to the rank of Commodore in the U. S. Navy, not contented with having abused his command by his coednct towards junior officers, has seen fit to convert his ship into a Livery Stable, for the purpose of speculating for his own private advancement, at the expense of the cortifort of his whole þÿship s company. On his return from the Mediterranean to Norfolk, the spaces between the guns were fitted up to accommodate twentytwo Jackasses and Horses with stabling, which were purchased at Malta at a price which would give a large return over cost when at home- The hint we had of a mutiny on board the Constitution, probably arose from the fact, that Com Elliot, instead of taking the ship up to Norfolk, (and discharging his men, whose term of service had expired some months, and who were anxious to get home.) stopped at Hampton to put out his cargo of cattle, even he perhaps being anxious to conceal the purposes to which his ship had been turned Had the vessel encountered an enemy in the condition she was, she could have been captured by a sioop of half her number of guns þÿ giving a fair opportunity for the scene of the Chesapeake and Leopard being re-enacted.

From the New York Evening Star, Sept. 4. PROGRESS OF ROYALTY. In our editorial article of Thursday, we called attention to the representative of the President at the English Court in the person of his eldest son. Fhe subject is one of deep import, and should excite the fixed and anxious attention of the American people. in the etiquette of Royalty, it is not the commission from the foreign office, from the department of state under the official seal, which gives rank and consequence, hut it is the perfumed letter signed by the þÿKing own s hand to his most beloved brother of Russia or Prussia, or Spain, or Turkey, which gives the bearer a' seat by the side of majesty, and a free and courtly entrance into the palace and amidst the stars and garters.

Tj83!TI5T2>33X maQWKfflllT1>3 AT23» Was not Mr. Van Buren long enough in London to learn this ? Did he not know that his own letter would be received and acted upon as from the head and chief of a great nation ? That the commission issued under the broad seal of the Union to Mr. Stevenson as resident minister, appointed by and with the consent of the Senate, and verified by the Secretary of State, would at the palace, by regal rule, sink into insignificance, when by the missive in his own hand he should present his son and heir as his delegate or legate at a coronation ? We ask our reader to cast his eye over the ceremony of that day. He will find the resident ministers the representatives of nations placed in the foreground of the procession þÿ a' ant courriers, with the soldiery to bre k through the crowd and announce to the bystanders at Westminster Hall, that Royal ty surrounded by the representatives of Kings is on the way, and in all good lime will be there to receive the congratulations and thanks ot subjects. Had Mr Stevenson one spark of old Virginia blood in bis veins, he would tear up his credentials and send home the mutilated and disgraced seal of the United States to the oliice from whence it issued, and with it a letter informing the American People that their minister, the þÿcountry s minister, can neither expect nor receive consideration wlnie tne President is allowed to sink the rank by sending forth his own son as ambassador to express his congratulations. If Mr. Van Buren, Jr. had any respect for his country þÿ

it he did not, with the feelings and notions ; derived from his father, hanker after rank, and court the smiles and attentions of those whose only merit aie their coronets and escutcheons, he would at once reject every attention, and would every where proclaim that the American Ministers alone is entitled to receive all the honors and distinction due to the country. He would say þÿ 1 am not the son of the President of the United States, the President has no sons ; I am the son of Martin Van Buren, Esq. if you please, and practising law at Albany, and have been sent out to England on professional business, or ain travelliug for curiosity or pleasure þÿ But no. Under the advice of his father he selects for the period ofhis arrival the coronation of the Queen, he claims rank as the nearest blood heir of the President þÿ he leaves our Minister to eat his joint of meat at a chop house in Downing street, while he is perched at the table, of fifty select covers, with his Royal Highness the Prince of Eslerliazy on one side, and a Bashaw with three tails on the other. All this shows the manner in which the youngman has been educated þÿ the school in winch he lias been brought up. His father, from the earliest period of our acquaintance with him, had a constant reaching after good society and artificial distinctions : lie despised while he cajoled the honest & industrious laborers of the country. When a resident at Albany, and while professional reputation had added little to his pocket, and political reputation

little to his consequence, you would find him resorting to all sorts of contrivances to fasten on to the skirts of what men called rich and genteel families, aping them in their manner and style. So it has always been. When the confidence ofhis fellow citizens had given him position at Washington he took Lis journey to Monticcllo to introduce himself to President Jefferson, then to the residence of

President Madison. He then journeyed through the Southern States, enquiring as he went along which were the most distinguished families, or the owners of the largest estates, and then sought and solicited their society.

The L.atb Gales. þÿ Our marine list for several days past, has presented a melancholy list of disasters at sea, caused by the late tremendous gales that have been experienced all along the coast. The weather has been particularly severe on the Viiginia and Carolina coast. A large number of vessels put into Norfolk to repair damages. It will be some weeks before the extent of the damages sustained can be fully known. Every mail from the South brings additional details of marine disasters The Insurance Companies in this city Philadelphia, and Boston, must have suffered severely. The gale appears to have commenced on the 3d of the month, some where in about lat. 33, long. 68, and to have gone to the south west. On the 7th it was experienced ofT Cape Florida in lat. 25, long. 68, from which point it ran up the coast as tar as New York, which it reached on the
itmi' i þÿ 'uii uwaiwmyy 12th, passing by Savanah and Charleston without much force. Its principal power appears to have been north of Cape Hatteras.

By the Southern mail we have further accounts of shipwrecks and distress hy the late gale they appear þÿ to have been much more extensive than at first apprehended. The Norfolk Beacon of the 21st contains an account of the loss of the sclir. Sarah Louisa, Smith, of and from New York, with a valuable cargo, bound to Mobile, she had spruug her foremast and lost several of her sails in the N. N. E. gale, and went ashore on Saturday morning, 15th Sept. on Whalehead, about 8 miles south of Currituck Inlet. The crew safe, the vessel bilged, embedded in the sand The crew of the schooner Louisa state that they saw ou the 7th day alter leaving New York, a brig apparently, Danish, dismasted. A brig, bottom up, drifted ashore on Kitty Hawks banks, about thirty miles south of Currituck. þÿ Ibid.

Arrival of a French Frigate. þÿ The French Frigate L'Astree, Commandant Garniet, (belonging to the West India station,) from Vera Cruz via Hanana 20 days from the latter," anchored in Hampton Roads on Friday night. The L'Astree was bound to Martinique, and encountered the late severe weather. As soon as she obtains a supply of provisions and water, she will proceed to her port of destination. A few days previous to her arrival in Hampton Roads she saw a vessel dismasted, when she run down, spoke, and inquired if they wanted assistance ; they made no reply. They ascertained that it was the brig May Flower, with stock on deck. þÿ Norfolk Beacon.

The Steamer Liverpool. þÿ We learn with much pleasure that Captain Favrer, so long known and respected as the commander of the government mail packets between Port Patrick and Dongalhadoe, has obtained the command of Sir John Tobin's new steain vessel, the Liverpool, which is appointed to sail from Liverpool for New York on the 1st of October. The splendid vessel measures 1 100 tons, is 237 feet long, being 14 inches longer than the Great Western ; she is 464 horse power, 76 inch cylinder, and 7 feet stroke. She has two sets of boilers, one set before, and the other set abaft the engines, so that they may be used either singly or together as circumstances may require, whether for cleansing one set while the engine is generating steam, or both, when full power is required. The command could not have devolved upon a more competent officer. þÿ Lieut. Favrer was first lieutenant of a frigate on the West India station during the whole of the American war, commanded by one of the smartest officers and best sailors in the navy ; he has been severely wounded in the service þÿ is practically and theoretically acquainted with steam navigation, and has lately invented a most ingenious plan for preventing or extinguishing fire in steam vessels, which has met the approval of the government and the most experienced engineers. þÿ To crown all, Captain Favrer is perhaps one of the best navigators and lonarians afloat, and was for several years since the peace, in command of Last Indiamcn.

The Company have ordered one thousand tons of coal from Liverpool and Scotland, which are now on the way to this port to supply the British Queen. The steam ship President building by the same company, was in frame, and was expected to be ready for her station in the line in the course of next summer or winter at farthest.

From the Glasgow Herald, Sept. 25, 1838. A great agricultural meeting and Cattle Show took place in Glasgow September 24th, attended by a numerous concourse of the Nobility and Gentry of Scotland; þÿ upwards of 1700 persons sat down to dinner at which the Cuke of Sutherland presided þÿ Mr Stevenson, Minister from the United States, was among the invited guests, and after the usual regular toasts, the noble chairman gave ' Prosperity to the United States of America and the health of Mr. Stevenson the American Minister," þÿ Drank with tremendous cheering ;-- Mr. Stevenson on rising was hailed with reiterated plaudits. He said þÿ Gentlemen, it would be an unworthy affectation in me if 1 did not say that I feel deeply sensible of the honour conferred upon me bv your Noble President in drinking my health, and associating my name with that of my country. Sirs, it is an honour less gratifying only than the kind and flattering manner in which the sentiment has been received by you, 1 thank you, in the first place, in the name of my ' country -(cheers) þÿ and if 1 may be permitted to be so tar led by my feelings as to suppose that any portion of personal kindness to nie dictated the toast þÿ then I would venture to thank you for myself. þÿ (Great cheering ) 1 must believe that in drinking prosperity to my country, you intended to convey by it even a higher and nobler sentiment, and that that was for the continuance of the kind and friendly relations which exist between your country and my own. (.More cheers ) Sirs,

if 1 am not mistaken in this sentiment, then permit me on the part of my country, and on the part of its government and people, to respond that sentiment, and to wish that perpetual friendship may subsist between Great Britain and America. (Loud and continued cheering ) Sirs, if our governments are wisely administered, and if the men who rule the destinies of both know what is good for both, and for the interests of mankind, that peace will be eternal, (Renewed cheering.) And no American or British Minister can take much merit to himself in wishing perpetual friendship, and promoting peace between the two countries. Sirs, it has been said that interest is the mighty bond that can alone unite nations together ; and if it be so, where aie there any two countries on the face of the earth that ought to be so closely united in the bonds of peace and friendship? Where is there any country in the Western world, or in the old one or what spot is there where, þÿ more than in your own noble and enterprising city the value of peace and its concomitants are so much known and appreciated ? þÿ Sirs, it is not interest which binds my country to yours, interest ! it may be a strong bond between others ; but there are a thousand kindly influences which are calculated to unite the mother and the daughter in the bonds of peace. (Cheering,) Sirs, we have sprung from common British ancestors þÿ (tremendous cheering) þÿ we speak the same language, we have the same manners, the same

religion we worship the same God, and arc of the same common stock (More cheering.) 1 feel the toice of the sentiment which I now express, for I know it to be true, that the greatest misfortune which could befal mankind would he a rupture between Britain and the United States. (Great cheering ) Sirs, as a representative of that country, 1 have

come here to do what little good I can in preserving those peaceful relations which now happily exist between us ; and I cannot better fulfil t lie wishes and expectations of my country, or of its government, than in doing every thing in my power, both officially and personally, to preserve and invigorate those relations on the preservation of which depend the honour and the prosperity of both. þÿ (Cheers ) I came with these sentiments þÿ 1 have been among you I have endeavoured þÿ to propagate them on all occasions, and I shall continue to do so as long as I remain the representative my country. (Cheers of ) Ii 1 am not guilty of trespassing I will say a word in relation to one or two other topics. (Cheers ) 1 respond cordially to the sentiments of your noble and illustrious President, the Noble Duke on my left hand, when 1 bear evidence to the value, in another country, viz. my own, of institutions like that which 1 have had the happiness and pleasure this day to witness. There is no division of opinion in my country as to the benefit flowing from these Societies. Upon the institution of Agricultural Societies and Cattle Shows depends the prosperity of the farmers in my country. Until their establishment in Ame rica, and I am sure in Scotland also, what was the situation of the farmer and husbandman ? Did he not want means of encouragement? Had he the public press ? Did the farmers hold assemblies to converse and consult with each other like the clergy? Did they assemble like the lawyers, who meet to

promote their own interest and advantage? No ; you had none of these advantages you þÿ had no means of meeting and co-operating together, for you lived not in cities, but were scattered over the face of the whole country, without any interchange of opinion or sentiment. But the moment that Scotland began this work, how soon was every thing changed ! You then had the mighty lever þÿ the Press, þÿ and, benefited by the periodical expression of your opinions, you could meet at your Cattle Shows, and exchange your sentiments þÿ your energies were roused, and you gathered around you the lords of the land. (Cheers.) I have read much of your Shows, at one of which I have now been accidentally presenl, and it h is indeed exceeded my most sanguine expectations: and 1 will not only profit by it as an individual, but endeavour to lead my country, through my influence, to profit bv it also. (Cheers.) Though this is my first visit to your country 1 must be permitted to say it will not be with my consent if it be the last. (Cheers.) am descended in one line from a Scotchman, and in this my first visit to the home of my ancestors, I must confess I never should have known what Scotland was unless 1 had come among you. 1 have been in every part of your country þÿ in the Highlands and in the Lowlands þÿ and every thing I have witnessed has delighted me. (Loud cheering.) If I have derived satisfaction from pouring over the crowded page of the chronicles of the olden time, what must I have felt in going over the country

they have immortalised þÿ going over your classic ground, the highlands, and traversing that region where men could point to the "lion heart and the eagle eye," with its theatres consecrated by the strains of your patriot bards, and the memory of your orators and plHlosophers þÿ cheers þÿ the most delightful visit to your country has been that of the last few days ; and may 1 assure you that I will go from you to cherish your institutions and your country, with a heart which, when

I am far distant, will lend me to look hack ttf to this with delight. Cheers. A land is your's which in the language of one of your poets þÿ who, if no other had lived, would have immortalized it þÿ is the " Land of the mountain and the flood," and I will add to it and say, is the " Land of the free and the home of the brave." An ancient clergyman one evening became the subject of conversation, and a wonder was expressed that he had never married " That wonder,' said M;ss Porter, " was once cxmessed to the rev. gentleman himself in my hearing, and he told a story in answer which i wiU tell you ; and perhaps, slight as it may seem, it is the history ol other hearts as sensitive and delicate at his own. Soon after his ordination, he preached, once every Sabbath, for a clergyman in a village not twenty miles from London. Among his auditors, from Sunday to Sunday, he observed a young lady who always occupied a certain seat, and whose close attention began insensiblv to grow to him an object of thought and pleasure. She left the church as soon as service was over, and it so chanscd that lie went on for a year without knowing her name ; but his sermon was never written without many a thought how she would approve of it, nor preached with satisfaction, unless fie read approbation in her face. Gradually lie came | Strand Street in this Town, belonging to the to think of her at other times than when writing sermons, and to wish to see her on other days than on Sundays ; but the weeks slipped on, and though he fancied that she giew paler and thinner, lie never brought himself either to ask her name or to speak wiih her. By these silent steps, however, jovc had worked into bis heart, and lie made up his mind to seek her marry iter if possible, when one dav be was sent for to minister at a funeral. The face

of the corpse was the same that had looked up to him Sunday after Sunday, till he Lad learned to make it a part of his religion and his life. He was unable to perform the service, and another clergyman present officiated ; and aficr she was buried, her father took him aside and begged bis pardon for giving him pain, but lie could not resist the impulse to tell him, that his daughter had mentioned his name with her last breath, and be was afraid that a concealed aficction for him had hurried her to the grave. From " the Barbadian" of the 14th instant, we extract, as far as our limits will permit, portions of the Earl of Durham's proclamation to the Canadians, resigning his high station of Gov. General of British North America, they are as follows, (after noticing the Act of indemnity of the British parliament and proclaiming the same HisLordship says :) " I cannot perform these official duties without at the same time informing you, the people of British America, of the course which the measures of the imperial Government and Legislature make it incumbent on me to pursue. 1 he mystery which has heretofore too often, during the progress of the most important affairs, concealed from the people of these colonies, the intentions, the motives) and the very action of their rulers, appears to me to have been one of the main causes of the numerous errors of the Government, and the general dissatisfaction of the people. Undesirable at any time, such concealment on the part of one entrusted with the supreme authority in the present crisis of your affairs, would be most culpable and pernicious. However hermetically Russia mav seal its frontiers, it cannot hinder us from obtaining here occasionally from the interior more particular accounts ot its relations and gainin' insight into its policy. The politique paeijiqua, as it is styled, which Count Strogonoff give as a toast in London, looks almost like irony, because it becomes more and more evident that Russia and England have lor some time carried on war with each other. 1 iic English secretly assist the rebellious Circassians so effectually that they are always able to continue the contest ; which is more sensibly felt by the Russians, as they would long since have subdued the mountaineers, who are destitute of all means to carry on regular warfare, but now see themselves impeded in their enterprises beyond the Caucasus bv an ever- watchful though bv no means powerful enemy in their rear. On the other hand Russia is assembling considerable forces in the south of the empire, the twofold object of which is no longer a secret; for, while one part holds itself in readiness to go to Asia Minor to support the l urks, large b >dies of troops further to the east are to march to the south (though the news given in English journals of theis arrival at Teheran is. probably, premature, only Russian artillerymen having vet been sent to that place), taking a direction which opens to them the way to the most vulnerable point ol tiie Bii-

þÿti h power It is, besides, not improbable, that the Russians may prefer the commercial route, by way ot Khiva, with which they are far better acquainted, to that through irak ; for the former is shorter, less dangerous, and more natural for the projects of þÿRussia. England is well aware of her weakness in India, and knows that the possession of this gigantic limb bv the dwarf European bodv can be hut transitory ; for as soon as the maxim teviile el impe.ru ceases to be applicable, that is as soon as the nations of India become sensible of their true interests, consequently then, considering the distance of the mother country and the great population of Hindustan, the empire of the English in

regeneration ot Asia can only proceed from her. I hence the reciprocal jealousy of the two nations, and especially of England, anxiously watching every step that Russia takes, or may take. It sees with alarming apprehension the Russian colussus advance, slowly indeed, but surely, to put an end to its unnatural supremacy in India. The rest of looks on this conflict with composure, and even with secret joy : for, on the one side, the sympathy of the continent for England is no where great and sincere, and, on the other hand, it must be satisfactory to Russia to j for have attention diverted from the west to the j east. If under existing circumstances the tianquillity of Europe is not interrupted, the | tie sole reason probably is that Russia does not see occasion to act offensively, but, prepared and wishing for the combat, waits till some other hand first takes the sword, to cut the Gordian knot of the policy of the east. Lord Palmerston evidently apprehends the first cannon shot; far, though not very clear sighted, he yet perceives the unavoidableness of this combat, which he probably only seeks to put off because he is aware of his own incapacity to guide the helm of England in a time of crisis. 1 ho British political edifice is too artificially put together to he kept proper in order, except by artificial means, the morality ot which, under these circumstances, must not bo too scrupulously thought of Great Britain may thank its week ministers that since the fall of Napoleon it has gradually declined in

iis political importance; had they continued in the course of their great predecessors, pioud England would have remained sole sovereign ot the seas, and would have no i ason to fear in the long run any nation upon earth. It- is true that its political consequence must not lie too strait laced (; but Uioy must buou, without direct occasion, take

the first step, and destroy at the onset every foreign naval power. The most favourable moment is now. perhaps, passed; for France, Russia and North America, possess fleets which may, indeed, be defeated, but cannot be annihilated. England too, ought long since to have recognised the Pacha of Egypt as an independent Sovereign, in order to gain a powerful and able ally in the East, whose well trained armies might be opposed to the projects of Russia. From the continental powers Russia has at present nothing to fear, for its policy is similar in its main outlines to that of theitreat powers of Eastern Europe, and Louis Philippe is not seated so firmly on his throne as to venture a war and its chances. The Euxine and the Baltic may be in a certain sense closed ; and it is possible lhat it was not merely for his amusement that the Emperor Nicholas made a voyage to Stockholm and guaranteed the succession to Prince Uscar The misunderstanding between Turkey (already so dependent on Russia) and its too powerful vassal the Pacha of Esrypt, must soon come to an issue. The status quo cannot possibly continue. The necessity of reducing the Diuses in Lebanon and Antilebanon lias propablv hitherto prevented the Pacha from proclaiming his independence. As soon as Mehemet All draws the sword, the Sultan must of necessity throw himself into the arms of Russia, upon which England will immediately separate itself from the Porte, recognise the independence of Egypt, and hasten to support the Pacha with
its power.

This grand banquet took place on Friday, aud excited in the City, and not in the City only, but in the diplomatic, political, and fashionable circles of the metropolis, a degree of interest greater than could have been expected to attach to any entertainment at Guildhall so soon after the splendour and the enthusiasm which distinguished the 9th of Nov. of last year, the day of her þÿMajesty s visit to the City. The preparations at the Guildhall for the reception of the illustrious guests of the coronation differed in a very slight degree from those which commanded general approbation on the occasion of the þÿQueen visit. s The company began to arrive soon after five þÿo clock ; and as the various distinguished guests were announced in succession it was easy to perceive, although any loud or tumul tuous expression of feeling was very properly discouraged, the various degrees in which our foreign visitors, and the public men of our own country engaged the attention and enjoyed the favour and sympathy of the mass of guests who formed an avenue for their advance act oss the hall to the steps leading to the Council Chamber, which was fitted up. as on the occasion of the þÿQueen v s isit, for a reception room, in which the Lord Mayor and Aldermen offered their welcome to their noble and illustrious visitors. Since the memorable era of 1813, when so many of the crown heads of Europe partook of a City banquet under the roof of this ancient and noble hall, we do not remember that

the sublime art of illumination has ever been exhibited with more effect than it was last night in the Guildhall of London. For the seasonable reason we have mentioned, the hall was not lit up prior to the arrival of the company, save only the two magnificent chandeliers, made bv Collins lor the Queen's visit in November. These, rat a very subdued state, were just alight, and many were the suppressed murmurs of some of the company at the time dinner was drawing to a close at the gloom which apparently threatened them. This, however, was evidently the intent and purpose of those who superintended this department; for on the health of our illustrious Queen being given, or rather on the last tremendous shout .of þÿ three times þÿthree, and the striking up of the national anthem, a blaze of light was poured fourth, as if by enchantment, from the Gothic windows at the end of the hall, as well as from the two chandeliers, which now were transformed from twinkling stars Into refulgent suns, highly rmblasoned with the royal arms in coloured glass. The effect was perfectly clcctical. The surprise and gratification experienced by the whole assembly was extreme, and was loudly and vehemently expressed by not a few of the royal and illustrious personages at the cross table. To complete the illumination, all the cornices and Gothic compartments, from one end to the other, were, in like manner, and with great rapidity, delineated in streams and gems of light In a word, this chef-d'auvre
of gas illumination was accomplished in a way to reflect the greatest credit upon the Chartered Gas Company, who have brought this invaluable ait to such a state of perfec-

One of the most splendid reviews held in the heighbourhood of the metropolis for many years took place in Hyde Park, before her Majesty and many other members of the royal family, the foreign ambassadors and ministers resident in this country, and the foreign ambassadors and ministers extraordinary, with their respective suits. Long before eight o'clock numbers of respectable people began assembling in the Park, and took up positions on the various seats and standings, for which sums varying from 6d to 5s were demanded, and cheerfully paid ; and by ten þÿo clock not a place was to be procured for either love or money. From Bull's Weekly Messenger, July 15. The Emperor of Russia reached Warsaw on the night of the 29th ult.. and held on the following day a review of the troops and garrison. The King of Prussia and his family arrived in Toplitz on the 2d inst., after devoting several days to visit the most picturesque sites of the mountains of Sileeia The Prussian court was thence to proceed to Furstenstein, where the Emperor of Russia was expected on the 13th, to celebrate the birthday of the Empress. The trial of Lieutenant Laitv, for having published a treasonable pamphlet advocating the claim of Louis Buonaparte to the French throne, came on before the Court of Peers on Monday last, and was concluded on Tuesday, when that officer was condemned to a detention of five years, a fine of 10,000 francs, and to the degrading surveillance of haute police during his lifetime. The Journal de la Haye states that the Germanic Diet has consented to cede part of the Grand Duchy of Luxembourg to Belgium, on condition of receiving a territorial indemnity from the King of Holland

Coronation of the Emperor of \itstria. The Emperor of Austria has recovered from his attack of the measles, and holds Steadfast to his purpose of being crowned at Milan as King of Lombardy. His coronation will be the more joyous as it will be an occasion of thanksgiving to Heaven for his recovery from a complaint so dangerous, at his age, as the measles is The present Emperor has an extraordinary predilection for pageants. He has been long since crowned King of Hungary, still more recntly King of Bohemia, and after September next his reign will present the singular instance of a thrice-crowned Sovereign.

(FROM OCR PRIVATE CORRESPONDENT.) BRISTOL. July 8. Half past Five þÿo Clock, p. m. The Great Western steam ship, Captain Hoskin, R. N., commander, cast anchor tins | afternoon in King-road, at about hall-past two o'clock, having performed the homeward passage in the wonderfully short space of 12 and a-half days The outward bound voyage was by this splendid vessel accomplished in 1 4 1 davs; having sailed from Bristol June 2nd, and reached New York June 17, at lour a in., which place she left for Bristol, June 25, at five p. m. Thus she has performed the whole vovage from Bristol to New York, and back again, in the unparalleled short space ol 39 days, eight of winch were spent at New York, which leaves her live weeks for the actual voyage, and which generally averages as many months by sailing vessels. The Great Western has brought over 92 passengers all of whom express themselves in terms of the greatest delight anil satisfaction with the splendour and comfort of her accommodations, and seem quite enraptured in making mention of the very slight motion felt on board the vessel throughout the passage, even when blowing hard, and during the latter part of the voyage they encountered heavy weather, which gave them an opportunity of judging of the great advantages possessed by the vessel in this respect. A passenger, with whom 1 had an opportunity of conversing, (

told me he had several times crossed the Atlantic in sailing packets, and in very similar weather to that experienced on his voyage home in the Great Western, and that he should not have believed it possible for such a difference to exist, had he not felt and tested it himself Even in the roughest weather it seems that passengers may sit down to dinner without any of the fears or dangers of accident on board sailing vessels. You feel assured that you will not be laid sprawling on the cabin floor by your chair lurching to leeward, or that you will be thought desirous of appropriating to yourself more than your share of eatables by getting the contents of half-a-dozen or more dishes poured wholsaie into your lap. None of these or other somewhat similar, but even more disagreeable accidents, so frequent but unavoidable on ship board, are here felt ; in fact, you may sit down and enjoy yourself almost in as much ease as in a drawing-room ori shore. This comparative tranquility and slightness of motion is mainly to be attributed to her great length, which enables her to cut through several waves into the troughs of which shorter vessels must of necessity roll, and become, as it were, þÿ swallowed þÿup Vessels of great length must, therefore, of course, by reason of their powers, not only be much easier, but must also save very considerably in the time and distance occupied by vessels of ordinary length in rising and falling from the troughs of these seas. þÿ OOo« þÿ

BONDS OF THE UNITED STATES BANK AGAIN. It appears that notwithstanding the fire that has been kept up by the Globe, and other i kindred papers, on the United States Bank. that the Government aiui Mr. Biddle have

mot on fair terms. The Bank had given their Bonds payable at a length of time ahead and bearing an interest, for the Stock held by the Government, at one hundred and fifteen dol Jars a share. Thus the Government have received fifteen per cent, þÿpremium a pretty round profit for þÿ Stock in an Institution which has been alledged, over and over again, to be insolvent The Government, however, were under the necessity of disposing of these Bonds to meet their current expenses. Mr. Biddle has not hesitated to meet them with an accommodating spirit, and has taken all the Secretary of the I reasury had to dispose of, at par. Thus the Government loses nothing in the sale, and the Bank taK< s its own Bonds, and. consequently, puts a stop to any further payment of interest. This shows, that not only has the Bank no disposition to be unfriendly, but that it has great strength as well as power. The Government must be greatly benefitted, as well as relieved, bv this sale They will now lie able to go on without embarrassment until Congress assembles, and it is to be hoped that the bitterness of the administration papers will be in some decree softened. The arrangement is one that must he beneficial to the public, as the constant agitation that has been þÿ Xperienccd will be allaved. Mr Biddle has shown in this transaction a generous and liberal spirit, one that will redound greatly to his own character fi-r moderation and firmness, and. at the same time, he lias shown himselt to be an able and accomplished financier.

DREADFUL MORTALITY AMONG THE NORTHWEST AMERICAN INDIANS- Extract from a letter from Major Pilcher, dated St. Louis, Feb. 27, 1838, to Gen. Wm. Clark. Superintendent of Indian Alfairs. þÿ Having received authentic information from the remote regions of the Upper Missouri of a highlv important character, 1 deem it my duty to communicate it without delay, though not entirely applicable to my own agency, having, as 1 conceive it does, a bearing upon Mr. Harriss letter of the 11th ultimo. « It appears that the effects of the small- pox among most of the Indian tribes ot the Upper Missouri surpases all former scourges, and that the country through which it has passed is literally depopulated, and converted into one great graveyard. The Mandans, consisting of 1000 souls, had been reduced, by the first of October last to þÿsons. tribe about 1000 strong, took the disease a month later than their neighbours, the Mandans. One half had perished, and the disease was still raging. They, no doubt, shared the same fate with the Mandans. 1 he Ricaras, who had recently joined the last named tribes, and numbered about three thousand, were most ot them out on a hunting excursion when the disease broke out among the Mandans, and consequently received it something later. One half of them had fallen, and the disease was raging with unabated lurv, not more than one out of fifty recoverin'' subsequently C from it. Most of those that survived committed suicide, despairing, ... 1 suppose at ihe loss of friends, and the changes wrought by the disease in their persons

some by shooting, others by stabbing, and some by throwing themselves from the high precipices along the Missouri. 1 he great band of Assinanebois, say 10,000 strong, and the Cress, numbering about 3000, have been almost annihilated; and notwithstanding all the precaution used by the gentlemen engaged in the trade of that remote region to prevent it, the disease had reached the Blackfeet of the Rockey Mountains; a hand of J000 lodges had been swept off, and the disease was rapidly spreading among the diflerent bands of that great tribe numbering, l think, about 00,000 souls. I have no doubt that the predictions contained my letter in of the 27th ult. will be fully realized, and all the Indians on the Columbia river, as far as the Pacific ocean, will share the fate of those before alluded þÿto. This is a fearful description of deplorable suffering among the red men. It is gratifying to know that as soon as authentic accounts of the ravages of the small pox among the tribes in the Missouri were received, inquires were promptly instituted by the proper authorities to ascertain their origin and extent, and measures adopted to afford alleviation, and, where practicable, to prevent further infection. Funds for vaccinating the ludvaiu were im-

mediately remitted, with authority to employ the execution of these measures posses. grea the necessary ngents. The agent charged s wit . energy, and the most favourable results may be anticipated. þÿ New ) ork Mercantile A vertiser.

TO THE AUTHOR OF THE þÿ ADDRESSES TO THE QUEEN Off THE POLITICAL DOCTRINES OF JOHN HORNE þÿTOOKE. Mv dear Sir, In your address to her Majesty, published in the Sunday News of the 24th ultimo, you have endeavoured to stive to the Queen that information respecting the late grand demonstration of the public- mind at Glasgow, which it is ot high importance that her Majesty should have, but which the whole of the daily press has studiously endeavoured to conceal from her eyes, and from those of the public. I now trouble you with a Newcastle- upon- Tyne Paper, ot 30th ol June, by which you will perceive that a demonstration, scarcely inferior in importance, has also taken place there; at which it appears that not less than from (50,000 to 80.000 men were present, who conducted themselves in a peaceful, firm, and legal manner, although illegally surrounded and insulted by soldiers, consisting of horse, foot, and artillery. This great and important meeting has not been noticed by the Daily .Press, which I have often called þÿ the. best possible public D ELUD Eli." At both these great Meetings, and at twenty others which have been equally concealed from the public knowledge, the Great National Petition, recommended by the Birmingham Political Union in May last, has been unanimously adopted and enthusiastically approved.

am informod has been signed already by 70. 000 men at Glasgow ; and l am sure that it will give you satisfaction to perceive that among the great rights claimed bv the people are included those two great constitutional principles to which you first directed our attention in our Birmingham Petition of Rights of the 13th of December, 1830, viz: the payment of þÿ the wanes ol attendance to þÿ members of the House of Commons and the abolition of the properly qualification ol members, which was unknown to our History and Constitution until the statute of Anne. 1 remember that when you fust þÿ drew out from the ancient storehouse of our þÿConstitution, as l then expressed it, these truly great and invaluable principles, they were not at first properly appreciated by the public mind, although enthusiastically approved by the men of Birmingham. I now congratulate you upon their rapid progress in the public estimation ; and 1 cannot but express my anxious hope that von may yet live to see them again embodied in the practice of our Constitution, and contributing with the other doctrines of your þÿ great þÿmaster, as you call him, John Horne Tooke, in securing stability and glory to the throne, and liberty, happiness, and contentment to the people. I am, mv dear Sir, Yours, ever faithfully, THO HAS ATTWOOD. St. G enrge's Terrace, Gill July, 1838.

GRAND NATION A L DEMONSTRATION. The following is the þÿ Grand demonstration of the public þÿmind, referred to by Mr. Attwood in his letter in The News of this day : þÿ 1. That the Reform Bill having failed to realise practical benefit to the people, it has become absolutely for the masses again to exert their power in procuring those political rights, and that voice in the election of representatives, which is the inalienable inheritance of Britons, and which can alone secure a fair remuneration lor labour, and the peaceable possession of property. 2. That as every man is obliged to contribute to the support and defence of the Stale, every man is entitled to a vote in the election of those appointed to control the management of .State affairs ; therefore the suffrage should be as universal as in the support demanded. 3. That in voting for representatives, 1 send you a copy of this petition, which I | every man is entitled to the uncontrolled exercise of his own judgment, alike free from the violence of power, and the corruption of wealth ; and, therefore, is the secresy and

necessary. 4. That the duties of a representative are numerous and burdensome, and as it is neither just nor safe in matters of importance to accept of gratuitous service, every representative should be paid for his labour ? and, farther, to secure attention to the duties ol his station, should be elected annually. 5. That as free trade is essential to the prospeuty of Great Britain, corn-laws and commercial restrictions are highly injurious, and should be forthwith repealed. 0. That in accordance with the above resolutions, the following national petition be adopted, numerously signed, and the commilee forwarding the demonstration appointed to carry the same into eticct, as also empowered to send a delegate to London to act in concert with those deputed from other parts of the country for a similar purpose. þÿ Unto the Honourable the Commons of .the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland in Parliament assembled, the Petition ol the undersigned, their suffering contrymen, Humbly Sheweth, þÿ That We, your petitioners, dwell in a land whose merchants are noted for enterprise þÿ whose manufactmesare very skilful and whose workmen are proverbial lor their industry. > The land itself is goodly, the soil rich, and the temperature wholesome; it is abundantly furnished with the materials of commerce

i »nir and trade ; it has numerous and convenient harbours ; in facility of internal communication it exceeds all others. þÿ For tliree-and-twenty years we have enjoyed a profound peace. þÿ Yet, with all these elements of national prosperity, and with every disposition and capacity to take advantage of them, we find ourselves overwhelmed with public and private suffering. þÿ We are bowed down under a load of taxes; which, notwithstanding, fall greatly short of the wants of our rulers ; our traders are trembling on the verge ol bankruptcy ; our workmen are starving; capital brings no profit, and labour no remuneration ; the home of the artificer is desolate, and the warehouse of the pawnbroker is full ; the workhouse is crowded, and the manufactory is deserted. þÿ We have looked on every side, we have searched diligently, in order to find out the causes of a distress so sore and so long continued. þÿ We can discover none in nature, or iu providence. þÿ Heaven has dealt graciously by the people. but the foolishness of our rulers has made the goodness of God ot none effect. þÿ The energies of a mighty kingdom have been wasted in building up the power of selfish and ignorant men, and its resources squandered for their aggrandisement. þÿ The good ol a party has been advanced to the sacrifice of the good of the nation ; the few have governed for the interest of the lew ; while the interest ol the many has been neglected, or insolently and tyrunnously trampled upon. þÿ It was the fond expectation of the people

that a remedy for the greater part, if not for the whole, of their grievances would be found in the Reform Act of 1832. þÿ They were taught to regard that act as a wise means to u worthy end ; as the masecurity of the Vote by Ballot imperatively t chiaery of an improved legislation, where the will of the masses would be at length potential. þÿ They have been bitterly and basely deceived. þÿ The fruit which locked so fair to the eve, has turned to dust and ashes when gathered. þÿ Flie Reform act has efiected a transfer of power from one domineering faction to another, and left the people as helpless as before. þÿ Our slavery has been exchanged lor an apprenticeship to liberty, which has aggravated the painful feeling of our social degradation, by adding to it the sickening of still deferred hope. þÿ We come before your honourable house to tell you, with all humility, that this state of things must not he permitted to continue ; that it cannot long cuntinuc without very seriously endangering the stability of the throne and the peace of the kingdom ; and that if. by þÿGod help s and all lawful and constitutional appliances, end can be put to it, an we are fully resolved that it shall speedily come to an end. þÿ We tell vour honourable house, that the capital of the master must no longer he deprived of its due profit ; that the labour of the workman must be no longer be deprived of its due reward? that the laws which make þÿ food dear, and those which, by making money

scarce, make labour cheap, must be abolished; that taxation must be made to fall on property, not on industry ; that the good of j the many, as it is the only legitimate end, sn i must it be the sole study ol the government.

þÿ As a preliminary essential to these and Other requisite changes ; as the means, by which alone the interests of the people can be effectually vindicated and secured, we demand that those interest be confined to the keeping of the people. þÿ When the State calls for defenders, when it calls for money, no consideration of poverty or ignorance can be pleaded in refusal or delay of the call. þÿ Required as we are, universally, to support and to obey the laws ; nature and reason entitle us to demand, that, in the making of the laws, the universal voice shall be implicitly listened to. þÿ We perforin the duties of freemen ; we must have the privileges ol freemen. « Wk dkmanu Universal Suffrage. þÿ The suffrage, to be exempt from the corruption ot the wealthy, and the violence of the powerful, must be. secret. þÿ The assertion of our right necessarily involves the power of its uncontrolled exercise. « VVe ask for the reality of a good, not for its semblance. þÿ We demand the Ballot. « The connection between the representatives and the people, to be beneficial, must be intimate. þÿ The legislative and constituent powers, for correction and for instructions, ought to be brought into frequent contact. Errors, which are comparatively light when susceptible of a speedy popular remedy, may produce the most disastrous effects when permitted to grow inveterate through years of compulsory enderance. þÿ To public safety, as well as public confidence, frequent elections are essential

þÿ We demand Anneal Parliaments. þÿ With power to choose, and freedom in choosing, the range of our choice must be unrestricted þÿ We are compelled, by the existing laws, to take for our representatives men, who arc incapable of appreciating our diifieulties, or who have little sympathy with them ; merchants who have retired from trade, and no longer feels its liarrassings ; proprietors of land, who are alike ignorant of its evils and their cure ; lawyers by whom the honours of the senate are sought after only as a means of obtaining notice in the courts. þÿ The labours of a representative, who is sedulous in the discharge of his duty, are numerous and burdensome. þÿ is It neither just, nor reasonable, nor safe, that they should continue to be gratuitously rendered. þÿ We demand that, in the future election of members of your honourable house, t tie approbation of the constituency shall be the sole qualification; and that, to every representative so chosen, shall be assigned, out of the public taxes, a fair and adequate remuneration lor the time which lie is called upon to devote to the public service. þÿ finally, we would most earnestly impress on your honourable house, that this petition has not been dictated by any idle love of change ; that it springs out of no inconsiderate attachment to fanciful theories ; hut that it is the result of much and long deliberation, and of convictions, which the events of each succeeding year tend more and more to strengthen. The management of this mighty kingdom
lias hitherto been a subject for contending factions to try their selfish experiments upon.

a>jUTsr Tua'j'jgaasx jle mutant t>3 þÿ We have felt the consequences, in our sorrowtu! experience þÿ short glimmerings of uncertain enjoyment swallowed up by long and dark seasons of suffering. þÿ If the self-government of the people should not remove their distresses, it will at least remove their repinings þÿ Universal suffrage will, and it alone can, bring true and lasting peace to the nation ; we firmly believe that it will also bring prosperity. þÿ May it, therefore, please your honourble house to take this our petition into your most serious consideration ; and to use your utmost endeavours, by all constitutional means, to have a law passed, granting \ to every male of lawful age, sane mind, and unconvicted of crime, the right of voting for members of Parliament ; and directing all future elections of members of Parliament to be in the way of secret ballot ; and ordaining that the duration ol Parliament so chosen shall in no case exceed one year ; and abolishing all property qualifications in the members ; and providing for their due remuneration while in attendance on their Parliamentary duties. þÿ And your petitioners, James Turner, Esq., Thrushgrove, Chairman.

From the London News and Sunday Globe, July 22, 1838. At the last meeting of the council of the Birmingham Political Union Mr Attwood, alluding to the members of the House of Commons, observed þÿ " I must say of them, as politicians, that they are the worst set I ever knew assembled in that House. I have been in Parliament six sessions, and this is the third Reformed Parliament ; and, as far as I can judge of it, it is worse than the old borough mongering set. It has less sympathy with the interests of industry, and with the rights and liberties of the industrious classes ; and it is still more inditrerent to the foreign honour of the nation." A picture more faithful than this of the present constitution of the House of Commons was never yet drawn. Its members are, as politicians, the worst set that ever assembled." They are the mere slaves of faction. There are not twenty men in the House who can with truth be said to be in reality independent. On the one side we have the blind followers of Peel, on the other the mere creatures of Russell The line drawn between the Ministerial side and the Opposition was never so distinct. The leader of either faction can, with a nod, command the practical sacrifice of principle and honour. Political integrity is quite by the way þÿ it is utterly repudiated; nothing is held to be worth a thought which O O does not directly involve the existence of the government. The men of Birmingham, however, by whom, it appears, the example must always be set, are beginning þÿ to perceive that unless they awake from their dream of security the

representative system will be so strongly impregnated with corruption that nothing but a physical revolution will be able to render it pure. Their petition þÿ the National Petition þÿ which we inserted at length in the News, will, we learn from our own patriotic contemporary, the Birmingham Journal, be shortly complete with two millions of signatures ! þÿ It has been signed by seventy thousand men in Glasgow alone ! þÿ by forty thousand in Birmingham, and all the other large towns are now following their noble example. Petitions, however, are not alone sufficient. þÿ Meetings must be held in every town throughout the kingdom, that the feelings of the people may not be misunderstood. " I have no hope whatever," said Mr. Attwood, " but in the masses of the people ; and the difficulty and danger of bringing them into efficient action for the safety of the nation are tremendously great, Nevertheless, into such efficient action, peaceful, legal, and overwhelming in their power, the mighty masses of the people must be bromght."

TO THE WEEN. GREAT MEETING AT BIRMINGHAM AND MARSHAL SOULT. recollections of the political life and oeneral doctrines of john iiorne tooke, by one of his disciples. We are informed by the public press (Mr. Attwood's "best possible public detuder") that the great object of this old Bonaparte- General's visit to England, is to bring about a marriage between your Majesty and the Duke de Nemours. These addresses have abundantly proved, upon the authority of our great Master, that such a marriage may be Just as you please, and that you will have nobody but yourself to blame, if it shall be otherwise ; provided only that the Duke is

a>AH3K Tasstrirwaam aiastiaaiisasms ArJ3. ready to give proof of his conformity to the established religion of the land, according to one of the conditions in the Act of Settlement, and which no gallant young frenchman in these days could hesitate about tor one moment, nor think of asking the Pope's pardon for marrying lovely girl, a as old Talleyrand did upon his death-bed , but never before. þÿ Those who will stand by you protecting in you from marrying any man, be lie what he may, against your own free choice, and thereby becoming miserable perhaps all your lite, namely, the industrious millions of Englishmen, now about to assume an attitude worthy of their name, are too enlightened to be gulled with the speculative motives of politicians. Better, tar better, to remain single, as Queen Elizabeth did, at the head of your own people, than submit to the degradation of such doubtful policy as marrying against your will for the sake of forming foreign alliances ; from which, you may remember, our great Master proved the greatest mischiefs " had arisen at all times and in all countries." But if it be the policy of your ministers, as it ought to be, to do everything in their power, consistent with the dignity of the Crown, to strengthen the good understanding between France and England, there is a wide field open to them. Why do they not suggest to Marshal Soult, as this address shall, to be a spectator of one of tfiose great political meetings of the people of England, which Lord Holland, to his eternal honour, has boldly de-

clared, in his place Parliament, in and as a Minister of the Grown, "to be as much a part of the English constitution as the meetings of the House of Lords itself." Such an opportunity most fortunately presents itself to the Marshal in the great central meeting to be soon held at Birmingham. þÿ Here he will be able to form a pretty accurate idea whether it will ever be in the power of Tory or any other rulers to involve us again in an unjust war with France. Here he may learn with what chance of success he may lead his brave soldiers, backed by England, against Russia, and sweep that stronghold and focus of despotism from the surface of the earth. Let him recollect the axiom of his old master, Napoleon, as to the consequence of the gigantic views and of the aggrandisement of Russia to the south of Europe, Let him consider that the eldest brother of that great man Joseph Bonaparte, though at this moment doing us the honour to reside amongst us in the most retired and unostentatious manner, is as a lion couchant ; that he is a man who has, as is well known, " descended from two thrones without a stain," a man who is quite above seeking or wishing for power of any sort, unless the great majority of his countrymen called for his assistance to do good ; but a man who, in such a case, would fix the liberties and happiness, of France upon a rock, and whose very name in the cause of freedom would be like that of Nelson upon the seas. Let the Marshal ponder upon these things;

he was not bred up amidst the gewgaws of coronets or coronations. Let him see the sublime sight of a meeting of the levers of liberty in the heart of England. There he will hear no mawkish twaddle about the " blessings of peace" (it should be called the " miseries of peace") with the scourge and destroyer of Poland, and the would-be scourge and destroyer of England and France, and of every other country that .sighs lor liberty. þÿ Let him know thai the molto of the men of

Birmingham is " Armo virumque cano." Let him but once hear the sound of their cheering, so different from what he has heard in the streets of London, and lie will not forget it. He will have something worth carrying hack to the ears of Louis Philippe ; something that shall make him more desirous than ever, that his son should have succeeded in really winning the heart of your Majesty.

COURT AND FASHION. The Queen held a levee on Wednesday afternoon at St. James's Palace. His Royal Highness the Duke of Sussex, their Serene Highness the Duke of Saxe Coburg Gotha, K, þÿG the Duke of Nassau, the Hereditary Prince of Nassau, Prince Maurice of Nassau, Prince Christian of Holsiein, attended by M. de Bille, Chamberlain of his Danish Majesty, and Danish Minister to the Hanseatic Cities, and Count G. de Btueher, the Prince of Leiningen, and the Prince of Furstenburg arrived at the palace and attended the levee. The presentations were numerous. After the levee her Majesty held a privy council, which was attended by the Ministers of State. At the council a new great seal of England, executed from the design of Mr. Benjamin Wvon, was submitted to her Majesty in council, and was approved of. A proclamation was issued respecting the coinage, relative to the wear and tear, and the silver fourpenny pieces or groats. On Thursday night her Majesty gave a state ball, at the new palace, which equalled in brilliancy anv given this season. The marble hall and grand staircase, as on former occasions, were brilliantly illuminated and decorated with flowering plants and rare fragrant shrubs. With but one slight exception the arrangements were precisely the same as observed at the other balls given by her Majesty. The Princess Sophia, Duchesses of Kent and Gloucester, Duke of Sussex, and Duchess of Cambridge, were present. Dancing commenced five minutes before 11, In r Majesty opening the ball with his Royal

Highness Prince George of Cambridge. Her Majesty danced several times with noblemen of elevated rank. Her Majesty wore a rich satin dress, over which was a light laie tunic, trimmed with white roses and diamonds. On each arm was a white rose, confined wilh a cluster of brilliants. Headdress, a large white rose on the left side, the entire being formed of diamonds; a circlet of diamonds confined the hair. The drosses of the ladies were much more elegant than usual, from the many artificial flowers with the centres of jewels with which they were trimmed.

Departure of His Royal Highness the Duke de Nemours. þÿ His royal highness embarked at London- bridge, on Wednesday morning, at half-past eight for Boulogne, en route to Paris, where he would arrive on Thursday morning, and after receiving his orders, proceed to the camp at Luneville.

His Excellency Marshal Soult will leave town for Paris earlier than was at first con templated, the presence of the illustrious warrior being considcied indispensable at the celebration of that fetes of the three days ol July ; and it is doubtful whether he will remain for the Duke of Wellington's grand dinner to the foreign ambassadors on the instant.
